correctness.rationale: The defining signed-root support functions are exact, and strictness is governed by the ordered global extremum indices. Exact permutation counting gives the angular formula. Joint upper/lower Gaussian extremes in disjoint blocks are asymptotically independent Gumbels with log-proportion shifts, and the common radial factor gives intrinsic spherical scaling. Uniform integrability of centered Gaussian maxima and the exact Gaussian radial expectation factorization justify mean convergence. Max-stability and the sum-of-two-logistic integral give E D = -log(alpha beta)-1. The checker independently compared 750 signed-root support calculations, 5 complete rank arrangements, 4 Gumbel cases, and a 100000-cell midpoint quadrature. Limits do not rely on simulations.

originality.rationale: The precise signed-root support functions are classical consequences of the definition, and the joint upper/lower Gumbel limit is standard; neither alone asserts the present geometric comparison. The assessed claim adds the sharp nonnegative scaled width-loss law with its nontrivial zero atom, an all-finite-dimension angular probability and the evaluated mean coefficient -log(alpha(1-alpha))-1. The available complete-bipartite primary papers focus on facet counts, triangulations, h* invariants, and metric identifications, while the compared mathematical records address inradii, ellipsoids, one-skeleton spectra or graphical zonotopes. The searches yielded no statement covering this combined width-loss law. The risk of a previously known equivalent Gaussian order-statistics identity is explicitly retained.

value.rationale: The two natural signed graph-root bodies have identical Euclidean circumradius and leading mean width despite removing all same-part edges. The theorem resolves a natural second-order geometric invariant, exhibits a nontrivial full distribution and atom at zero, gives exact finite-dimensional strict-angle probability, and evaluates a strictly positive imbalance-dependent coefficient. The precise K_n versus K_{p,q} contrast has clear mathematical motivation independent of computing it, and the answer is not implied by the common radius or by published lattice/face data.
